summary: CascadeWatch is a web app that lets anyone explore 46 years of NASA Earth observation data to investigate what is actually changing in Seattle's two drinking water watersheds — the Cedar River and the Tolt. We set out to prove the conventional wisdom: that Seattle is losing its snow. The data surprised us. Using Mann-Kendall significance testing on NASA NLDAS-2 model data, we found no significant trend in snowpack, winter temperature, or total precipitation in either watershed. What we did find is that late-summer runoff is falling about 14% per decade in both watersheds — a real, statistically significant trend confirmed across Cedar and Tolt (q < 0.05). That's the water Seattle pays peak rates for, arriving in smaller and smaller amounts every decade. CascadeWatch visualizes this story, lets users explore any variable and run their own trend tests, and makes the underlying data downloadable for deeper analysis.
details:
The Cedar River and Tolt River watersheds supply drinking water to roughly 1.6 million people in the Seattle metro area. Both are fed by snowpack in the Cascade Mountains. We set out to investigate the conventional wisdom — that Seattle is losing its mountain snow — using 46 years of NASA Earth observation data.

Our team extracted seven variables from NASA's Giovanni and AppEEARS platforms across five study regions: the Cedar watershed (whole, upper, and lower), the Tolt watershed, and the Seattle city area. The variables are snow water equivalent (SWE), snowfall, rainfall, runoff, near-surface air temperature, daily precipitation, and annual snow cover days. We applied Mann-Kendall significance testing with Hamed-Rao autocorrelation correction and Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate adjustment to each time series — meaning we only call a trend "real" when the data truly proves it, after correcting for testing many variables at once.

The result surprised us. Snowpack shows no significant trend in either watershed. Neither does winter temperature, rain fraction, or total precipitation. Our original hypothesis was wrong.

What is changing is late-summer runoff. In every region we studied — Upper Cedar, Lower Cedar, whole Cedar, and Tolt — summer runoff is falling at approximately 14% per decade, a statistically significant trend (q < 0.05) confirmed independently in both watersheds. That is roughly one in seven summer buckets of water lost every ten years. This is the water Seattle already pays peak rates for, from May through September.

We built CascadeWatch to make this findable by anyone. The app walks users through the story of how Seattle's water moves from snowflake to tap, shows the current water year at a glance, and lets users explore any variable across any year range with a live significance test. Users can compare two years month by month, download any dataset as a CSV, and see which trends are real, which are borderline, and which would take decades more data to prove. An impact section connects the data to low-snow years, late-summer river flow, and Seattle's tiered water billing structure.

CascadeWatch is built with React and Vite, with data processed in Google Colab using Python. All NASA data was sourced directly from Giovanni (NLDAS-2 Noah and Forcing) and AppEEARS (MODIS MOD10A2). The full codebase is open source under the MIT License.
